caseno: Appeal from Original order No. 184 of 1978.
lawyer:
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mahbubey Alam ----- For the Appellant 
Khademul Islam with S.M.H. Rahman ----- For the Respondent Nos. 1& 4
parties:
Mt. Aymun Nessa & ors ----- Appellants
vs.
Md. Obaidul Haque and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Altaf Hossain, J:- This appeal is directed against an order dated 30.9.78 passed in Title Suit No. 407 of 1978 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca allowing plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction and restraining the defendants from changing the nature and character of the suit property by making new constructions over any portion till disposal of the suit. 

 2. The respondent No. 1 as plaintiff filed the suit seeking partition of the suit property against the appellants and respondent Nos. 2 to 6 as defendants. The suit property comprising 3 items belonged to Abdul Khaleque who died leaving the appellant Nos. 1 to 6, plaintiff-respondent and respondent No.1 as heirs. The appellant No.7 and other respondents acquired interest by purchase. The plaintiff claimed 1/13th share in the property and prayed for separate saham on partition. In the suit, the plaintiff filed an application for temporary injunction for restraining the appellant-defendant from changing or altering the nature and character of the suit properly by making any constructions in item 2 till disposal of the Suit. 1 he appellant-defendants opposed plaintiffs' prayer for temporary injunction. The learned Trial Court on consideration of the cases of the respective parties and on perusal of all materials placed before him allowed plaintiffs prayer for temporary injunction. 

 In the appeal, at the instance of the appellants, a rule has been issued calling upon the plaintiffs-respondent to show cause why operation of the impugned order dated 30.9.78 should not be stayed till disposal of the appeal. An ad-interim stay has also been granted. 

 4. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellants submits that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in granting injunction restraining the beneficial enjoyment of the properties by the major co-sharers owing 12/13 share, who were in undisputed possession for long time. He further submits that the Trial Court has passed the order of injunction without considering the balance of convenience and inconvenience of the parties. The learned Advocate submits that the appellant-defendants have been making constructions in item 2. Items 1 and 3 are more than sufficient to cover the share of the plaintiffs and there is no reason why the appellants who are in exclusive possession of item 2 should be restrained from making their constructions. He submits that the impugned order is not sustainable in law. 

 5. Mr. Khademul Islam, the, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that the defendant-appellants were making construction in item 2 of the suit properties and changing the nature and character of the property as a result of which the plaintiff-respondent will be at a great disadvantage for getting her due at the time of partition. He submits that the learned Subordinate Judge has passed a well-considered order and it does not call for an interference by this Court. 

 First, the plaintiff has to establish a prima facie case. Secondly, it has to, be shown that the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss if the injunction prayed for is not "ranted and thirdly, the balance of convenience lies in favour of the plaintiff and in favour of granting the temporary injunction' prayed for. In the instant case, there is no dispute that the plaintiff is a co-sharer and has got a prima facie case for getting partition. It is now necessary to examine the other two points. The defendant-appellants are in exclusive possession of item 2 property and it is admitted that they have raised the ground floor of a super market in item 2. The appellant-defendants claim that they have spent about Tk. 7 lakhs in laying the foundation of the super market and have raised loans for making further constructions and have collected materials. The plaintiff has filed the suit for partition for getting her saham separated and her share is 1/3th. There are two other items and apparently the plaintiff can get a saham from the other two items Mr. Khademul Islam submits that the: property of item 2 is much more valuable then the properties of items 1 and 3. All the three items of property are in the same area and adjacent to the Air Port Road. Items 1 and 3 are a bit in the interior and even if it is held that item 2 is to some extent more valuable, the lands contained in items 1 and 3 will evidently be sufficient to cover the small share of toe plaintiff in case of a partition. It is evident that in case of a partition even if item 2 is entirely given to the appellant-defendants, items 1 and 3 remain available for the plaintiff and the plaintiff can be allotted her saham in those items. In the petition for temporary injunction, the plaintiff has nowhere averred that the quantity of land in items I and 3 are not sufficient to cover her share or that in case of item 2 going entirely to the appellants-defendant, she will suffer irreparable loss. An allegation or charge of this nature and character of one-item of property out of three items sought to be partitioned by itself and alone does not make out a case of irreparable loss and we are inclined to take a view that no case of irreparable loss has been made out by the plaintiff Coming to the question of balance of convenience, it appears that admittedly a super market is being constructed in item 2 and the ground floor has already been built. Defendant-appellants have already incurred huge expenditure and they have collected materials for further construction. If the constructions are restrained, the plaintiff does not stand to gain, but the defendants are apparently put to great disadvantage. Here we would refer to the decision of Israil vs. Shamsur Rahman reported in 4 ILR, Calcutta 4 6 relied on by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent. In that case some co-sharers filed a suit for declaration of title and for joint possession with a co-sharer who was in exclusive possession of the suit-land. The plaintiffs prayed for a temporary injunction and the Court held that under circumstances like those the matter for consideration at that stage was, where did the balance of convenience lie, was it desirable that the status quo should be maintained or was it right that the defendants should be allowed to continue to alter the character of the land. 

 7. That in the matter of granting temporary injunction that court has to consider where does the balance of convenience lie is 'an indisputable proposition of law. In the reported decision their Lordships of Calcutta High Court however appear to have been of the view that if a co-sharer in exclusive possession is allowed to make construction on the land of his possession the other co-sharers will be at a disadvantage. This, we would, with respects observe, can hardly be laid down as proposition of general applicability. Whether the co sharers not in possession are at a disadvantage is a question of fact which has to be gathered from the circumstances of each case. In the case before us, we have already found that in items 1 and 3 there in sufficient land to cover the share of the plaintiff. If the item 2 land entirely goes to the saham of the appellant-defendants in case of an eventual partition, there is no reason why the plaintiff cannot be given her full saham out of items 1 and 3 and there is no reason why plaintiff will be at a disadvantage It is evident if the defendant-appellants are not allowed to proceed with the construction they will be at a greater disadvantage. We are considering the advantages and disadvantages of co-sharers. The plaintiff has claimed 1/13th share and the appellant-defendants party are claiming 12/13th share. If the disadvantages could be quantified, it could be apparent that the disadvantages on the side of the appellants are much more than the disadvantages on the side of the plaintiff. The balance of convenience is apparently against the granting of temporary injunction. We being of this view, we have not been unmindful of the fact that substantial part of the constructions has been raised during the pendency of the suit including the appeal but we are unable to take a very harsh view against the defendants on that account.
